chapters.title: Chapter 3: Cointegration — Testing Whether a Pair Really Mean-Reverts

lessons.title: The Engle-Granger Two-Step Method for Testing Cointegration

children.text: You already have both pieces. Chapter 2 built a hedge ratio through OLS regression. Lesson 3 of this chapter tested a series for stationarity with the ADF test. The Engle-Granger method, named for Robert Engle and Clive Granger, whose work on this earned a share of the 2003 Nobel Prize in Economics, is simply the formal sequence of running these two steps together correctly, on the right series, using the right critical values. It is the standard, practical procedure for testing whether two stocks are cointegrated.

body.text: The Engle-Granger two-step method regresses one price series on the other to get a hedge ratio and a residual series, the spread, and then runs the ADF test on that residual series. The only real complication is that because the residuals come from an estimated regression rather than being observed directly, they need their own, stricter set of critical values, not the standard ADF ones.

children.text: This is exactly the regression from Chapter 2, Lesson 1: regress Stock A's price on Stock B's price over your chosen window, giving you a hedge ratio, beta, and the resulting spread, Stock A's price minus beta times Stock B's price. If you already built a spread earlier in this course, you have already completed this step.
Step 2: Test the Residuals for Stationarity

Run the ADF test from Lesson 3 on the spread itself. If the null hypothesis of a unit root is rejected, the spread is stationary, and the two stocks are considered cointegrated using the hedge ratio from Step 1. If the null cannot be rejected, the pair fails the test and should not be traded as a cointegrated pair on this basis, no matter how good the correlation or the regression fit looked.

cells: OLS regression of Stock A's price on Stock B's price
A hedge ratio (β) and a residual series (the spread)
ADF test on the residual series from Step 1
A test statistic and p-value, evaluated against Engle-Granger critical values

body.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import coint

# price_a, price_b: pandas Series of daily closing prices
t_statistic, p_value, critical_values = coint(price_a, price_b)

print(f"Engle-Granger t-statistic: {t_statistic:.2f}")
print(f"p-value: {p_value:.3f}")
print(f"Critical values (1%, 5%, 10%): {critical_values}")
body.caption: statsmodels' coint() function runs both Engle-Granger steps and applies the correct adjusted critical values automatically

children.text: Why the Critical Values Are Different Here

OLS regression, by construction, finds the hedge ratio that minimizes the residual variance, the smallest possible spread of leftover error. This means the resulting residual series is mechanically nudged toward looking as stable, and therefore as stationary, as the data allows, even before you have tested it for anything. Using the standard ADF critical values from Lesson 3 on this kind of estimated residual series makes it too easy to reject the unit root null and falsely conclude the pair is cointegrated when it may not really be. Engle and Granger derived their own, stricter critical values (further from zero) specifically for testing residuals from an estimated cointegrating regression, correcting for this bias.

body.caption: Standard ADF critical values vs Engle-Granger critical values (illustrative approximations, 2-variable case)

children.text: Revisit the worked example from Lesson 3: a test statistic of negative 3.42. Against the plain ADF 5 percent critical value of negative 3.00, that looked like a fairly comfortable rejection of the null. Against the correct Engle-Granger 5 percent critical value of negative 3.34, negative 3.42 still clears the bar, but only just, by 0.08. The conclusion, reject the null at 5 percent, happens to still hold here, but the margin is much thinner than the plain ADF test suggested, and a slightly weaker result could easily have flipped the conclusion entirely.

body.text: Never test a regression-based spread against the plain ADF critical values from Lesson 3. Always use the Engle-Granger critical values, or a function like statsmodels' coint(), which applies them for you automatically. Using the wrong table systematically makes pairs look more cointegrated than they really are.

children.text: A Known Limitation: Which Stock Goes on Which Side

Regressing Stock A on Stock B does not always give exactly the same residual series, or the same test result, as regressing Stock B on Stock A, because OLS minimizes error in only one direction at a time. In practice, this asymmetry rarely flips the overall conclusion for a genuinely strong pair, but it is worth testing both directions and using the one that gives the more negative, more significant test statistic, or picking the direction with clearer economic reasoning behind it, for example putting the less liquid or smaller-cap stock on the dependent side. More advanced methods, such as the Johansen test, handle this symmetrically and can test more than two series at once, but they sit beyond the scope of this course.

body.title: Which critical values to use
body.question: You have built a spread from an OLS regression of Stock A on Stock B and want to test it for stationarity. Which critical values should you use?
options: The standard ADF critical values from Lesson 3, since the ADF test itself has not changed
The stricter Engle-Granger critical values, since the spread is a residual from an estimated regression, not an independently observed series
Either set works equally well, since both test the same null hypothesis
No critical values are needed if the correlation coefficient was already above 0.7
body.explanation: Because the spread's hedge ratio was itself estimated by OLS, which mechanically minimizes residual variance, standard ADF critical values are too lenient when applied to it. The Engle-Granger critical values are specifically adjusted for this and are the correct choice for a regression-based spread.

body.title: A borderline result
body.scenario: Testing a candidate spread with the Engle-Granger method gives a test statistic of -3.10. The Engle-Granger 5% critical value is -3.34, and the 10% critical value is -3.02.
body.prompt: What can you conclude at the 5% level and at the 10% level, and what would you realistically do with this pair?
body.modelAnswer: At the 5% level, -3.10 is less negative than the -3.34 critical value, so the null hypothesis of a unit root cannot be rejected at 5%. At the 10% level, -3.10 is more negative than the -3.02 critical value, so the null can be rejected at the weaker 10% level. This is a genuinely borderline result: there is some evidence of cointegration, but not enough to meet the conventional 5% bar. A disciplined approach would be to treat this as inconclusive rather than tradeable, perhaps retesting with a longer data window or looking for a stronger candidate pair, rather than trading on a result this close to the edge.

cards.definition: The standard procedure for testing cointegration: (1) OLS regression to estimate a hedge ratio and residual spread, (2) an ADF test on that spread using critical values adjusted for the fact it comes from an estimated regression.
A stricter, adjusted set of critical values used when testing residuals from an estimated cointegrating regression, correcting for the bias introduced by OLS minimizing residual variance.
The tendency of standard statistical critical values to be too lenient when applied to a series (like OLS residuals) that was itself estimated from the data, rather than observed directly.
A more advanced cointegration test that handles the choice-of-direction issue symmetrically and can test more than two series at once. Beyond the scope of this course.

points: The Engle-Granger method is simply the regression from Chapter 2 followed by the ADF test from Lesson 3, run in sequence on the right series.
Because OLS regression mechanically minimizes residual variance, the resulting spread needs stricter, specifically adjusted Engle-Granger critical values, not the plain ADF critical values.
Using the wrong critical value table makes pairs look more cointegated than they really are, a subtle but important mistake to avoid.
Regressing Stock A on Stock B versus Stock B on Stock A can give different residuals and, occasionally, different test conclusions, a known limitation of this method.
A borderline test result, close to the critical value, is a signal to treat the pair as inconclusive rather than to trade it, not a reason to round up to "probably fine."
Passing the Engle-Granger test is the actual pre-trade bar this course has been building toward since Chapter 1. Lesson 5 runs this full process end to end on a real pair in Python.
